evidence: Suet. Aug. 24.2: cum ignōminiā tōtam dīmīsit

terms.comment: Classically to remove, take away (Lewis & Short).
Of soldiers, discharged with honour or in disgrace (Liv., Suet., Lewis & Short).

evidence: Suet. Caes. 69: missam facere legiōnem (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: decimam legiōnem contumācius pārentem cum ignōminiā tōtam dīmīsit, item aliās immodestē missiōnem postulantēs citrā commoda ēmeritōrum praemiōrum exauctōrāvit
phrases.english: the tenth legion, which obeyed with insolence, he dismissed in disgrace to a man, and others who demanded their discharge rudely he discharged without the rewards due for completed service

sources: Lewis & Short: dimitto · Lewis & Short: amoveo · Lewis & Short: exauctoro · Lewis & Short: mitto
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 305, 315.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. hire: fire, dismiss, terminate (someone’s) employment.
Suetonius, Augustus, checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
